docs.title: Native Decisions (Jev)
docs.text:
Status: one explicit production call site — the pantheon_jev_decide tool. This targets the OpenCode host native Decisions API, ctx.experimental.generate.decisions({ model, input, questions }), available from OpenCode 2.2.0 and exercised on 2.2.5. Pantheon targets current OpenCode hosts only; a host without the API simply does not register the tool. All Pantheon features are built for the current host generation — there is no legacy plugin line to consider.

The per-turn prompt hook remains local-only: no native call, no fetch, no provider request, no credential read, no prompt-content change, no permission narrowing, no agent dispatch, and no review/approval gate change. The local per-turn advisory recommendation is unchanged. The explicit Zeus-only tool below is the one consented production call site, running entirely through the host's own provider layer.

docs.title: Setup and decision models
docs.text:
Decision models are not chat models: they never appear in the host model catalog (opencode models) at all — field-measured on 2.2.5 (561 catalog entries, zero jev models, while the decisions API answers the same model ref directly). Route resolution therefore reads only your Pantheon config, never the catalog. Pantheon never maps or switches providers on your behalf.

Decision model Config candidate Host reference Billing / auth Route requirement OpenCode Console Jev opencode-console-jev / jev-1.13 { providerID: "opencode", id: "jev-1.13" } Zen workspace credits, via OPENCODE_API_KEY (a Go subscription does not include Jev — the host answers 404 without the workspace key) OPENCODE_API_KEY — host-native TypeSafe Jev direct typesafe-jev / jev-1.14.0 { providerID: "typesafe-ai", id: "jev-1.14.0" } Your TypeSafe key setup-model merges the complete custom provider entry into opencode.json (adapter, baseURL, apiKey: "{env:TYPESAFE_API_KEY}", type "decision"); then export TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<your key> and restart. /connect and opencode auth login do not carry custom providers — models.dev has no typesafe-ai entry OpenRouter-hosted Jev openrouter-jev / typesafe/jev-1.13 { providerID: "openrouter", id: "typesafe/jev-1.13" } OpenRouter credits (OPENROUTER_API_KEY; host-native models.dev provider — /connect supports it) None — host-native Vercel AI Gateway Jev vercel-gateway-jev / typesafe-ai/jev { providerID: "vercel-ai-gateway", id: "typesafe-ai/jev" } Vercel AI Gateway (AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY; host-native models.dev provider) None — host-native Cloudflare Workers AI (Clef) cloudflare-workers-jev / clef { providerID: "cloudflare-workers-ai", id: "clef" } Workers AI (CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN, scoped) Custom entry with your accountId — models.dev does not carry it; the Calibrated-Jev calibration does not transfer to Clef

Setup in one command (state lives in ~/.config/pantheon/decision-router.json, budget in ~/.local/state/pantheon/decision-budget.sqlite; the command requires explicit caps — there are no defaults):

npx pantheon-opencode decision-router setup-model opencode-console-jev/jev-1.13 \
  --monthly-usd 5 --per-decision-usd 0.10
npx pantheon-opencode decision-router doctor   # read-only verification with fixes

docs.title: Container & JupyterHub Environments
docs.text:
When running in containerized environments (such as JupyterHub, Docker, Kubernetes, or HPC clusters) where $HOME or ancestor directories are group-writable (e.g. /home/jovyan with mode 2775 root:users): - Pantheon automatically detects JupyterHub (JUPYTERHUB_USER, JUPYTER_IMAGE) and Kubernetes environments to permit group-writable ancestor directories. - In custom containers or environments, export PANTHEON_ALLOW_GROUP_WRITABLE=1 in your container environment or shell profile to permit group-writable ancestors while keeping the private 0700/0600 requirements on the leaf configuration and budget ledger files. - The decision-router status and doctor commands diagnose directory trust issues read-only and report actionable remediation hints instead of failing unhandled.

setup-model performs select + enable + consent + caps (user, provider, model) + period confirmation in one write and prints the verification checklist — and for the TypeSafe route it also merges the host provider entry into opencode.json (additive, idempotent). --no-consent configures everything except egress consent. doctor walks the whole native route — config, consent, selection, budget admission, unresolved holds, and a route-aware native-route check (host-native pass for the Console routes; provider-entry check for TypeSafe) — and prints the exact command to run for each failing gate. The per-command fallbacks (select, enable, consent, caps, period) remain for one-change-at-a-time edits.

docs.title: Ready-to-copy provider examples
docs.text:
The stock route needs no opencode.json change. The others do — merge (never replace) into your own config:

TypeSafe direct (your TypeSafe key; the catalog id must equal the config candidate's model). setup-model merges exactly this — or merge manually:

{
  "providers": {
    "typesafe-ai": {
      "npm": "@ai-sdk/openai-compatible",
      "name": "TypeSafe AI",
      "options": {
        "baseURL": "https://api.typesafe.ai/v1",
        "apiKey": "{env:TYPESAFE_API_KEY}"
      },
      "models": {
        "jev-1.14.0": { "name": "Jev (TypeSafe direct)", "modelID": "jev-latest", "type": "decision" }
      }
    }
  }
}

Then: export TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<your key>, restart OpenCode, and decision-router setup-model typesafe-jev/jev-1.14.0 --monthly-usd 3 --per-decision-usd 0.05. A models-only entry (no adapter/baseURL/apiKey) is inert: the host cannot resolve the provider and the decisions call 404s. /connect and opencode auth login list only registry (models.dev) providers — TypeSafe is not one.

OpenRouter-hosted Jev (billed by OpenRouter; the config candidate is not in Pantheon's matrix, so set an explicit selection through the host):

{
  "providers": {
    "openrouter": {
      "models": {
        "typesafe/jev-1.13": { "name": "Jev (OpenRouter)", "type": "decision" }
      }
    }
  }
}

Who can invoke: the orchestrator (zeus) always; allowlisted specialists for explicit typed questions only (owner/skill selection and result scoring stay orchestrator-owned). The allowlist comes from PANTHEON_JEV_SPECIALIST_CALLERS (CSV of agent ids, default empty = Zeus only; read at plugin registration). The permission assertion and the success output carry the real caller. Cost controls are the caps above (no defaults), the confirmed UTC period, and the host permission kill-switch on decision.egress — caps are enforced per call regardless of caller, so the allowlist is a consent-concentration policy, not a technical boundary.

docs.title: The explicit pantheon_jev_decide tool
docs.text:
Registered only when the host exposes BOTH the model catalog (ctx.model.list) and the native Decisions API. Execution requires the host tool context to identify the caller as Zeus, and runs this gate chain in order — every failure is a bounded refusal JSON, never a retry:

  1. Config gate — the user-level decision-router config must be enabled with egress_consent: true.
  2. Route gate — the selection (explicit, or auto with exactly one eligible candidate) must resolve to a native route through the frozen provider table. The host chat catalog is deliberately NOT consulted (decision models are not chat models); an unknown model surfaces as the host's own call error. Direct OpenAI has no native route and is never substituted.
  3. Budget gate — the ledger must admit a reservation (confirmed period, positive monthly and per-decision caps). The reservation is taken before the call and held (pending, fail-closed) if the call fails or the result cannot be reconciled.
  4. Permission kill-switch — ctx.permission.assert on decision.egress with the logical resource pantheon-native-decisions://<providerID>/<id>; a throw or explicit denial stops the call.
  5. Payload preparer — exactly one of:
  6. a preset: mode: "skills" (stack skills for the state text — the local prefilter shortlist when it matches, the whole catalog otherwise) or mode: "delegation" (every canonical specialist except Zeus);
  7. the review mode: mode: "review" (J4 output-quality scoring — shape metrics and named criteria in, a quality score and a needs-review flag out, advisory only; detailed below);
  8. the rank mode: mode: "rank" (v3.1 primitive — pick the best of 2–8 named candidates for the state; detailed below);
  9. the verify mode: mode: "verify" (v3.1 primitive — check 1–4 named claims; detailed below); or
  10. explicit questions: 1–4 typed questions (choice with 2–24 unique options, score with 2–10 unique levels, predicate), with bounded names, instructions, and descriptions.

The request carries only the state text (≤ 12,000 chars) as one text part. No files, history, system instructions, memory, or metadata are added. The state text is carried verbatim — it is not a secret-scanning boundary. 6. Host call — exactly one native Decisions invocation. Transport, credentials, and endpoints are entirely the host's; this path contains no fetch. 7. Settlement — the host-reported cost (USD) and token counts mint an opaque reconciliation capability; absent cost is a real zero (free variants). Cost above the reservation freezes the buckets. 8. Advice consumer — answers are validated against the prepared questions (one per name; choices must be from the prepared options; duplicates become errors) and returned with effect: 'none'.

The tool never dispatches agents, runs skills, executes other tools, grants permissions, or alters review gates.

docs.title: J1 risk-score gate (shadow)
docs.text:
A second, opt-in consumer of the same gate chain: when PANTHEON_J1_RISK_SCORE is set to 1, on, or true (anything else, or unset, leaves it off — and off means zero overhead: no sink, no observer, no per-call work), the plugin's execute.before hook fires ONE bounded native Decisions call per write/execute tool call — bash/shell and webfetch (execute), file writes (write). Read-only tools are never observed, and the target list intersects the secret scan's own exfil-capable gate, so a tool the scan never inspects is never observed either.

Each observation runs the exact chain the pantheon_jev_decide tool runs — config enabled + egress_consent, route via the budget ledger's admission check, the decision.egress permission kill-switch, one reservation, one host call, cost reconciliation — through the shared runner (runGatedNativeJevCall); no gate logic is duplicated. The request asks two questions only: one score ("risk of this tool call for the current task", 2–10 levels) and one predicate ("is this call consistent with the current task intent?").

Sanitization contract. The request carries NO user content: no task text, no file paths, no tool input values. The state text is a fixed template over three fields — the tool name (accepted only as a bounded [A-Za-z0-9._:-] token; paths, shell metacharacters, injection prose and oversize strings are rejected outright, never scrubbed), the scope class, and the sha256 of the serialized tool input (an opaque correlation value). The telemetry record carries the outcome as one bounded reason token, e.g. risk-3-intent-yes or skip-timeout.

Fail-open and fail-silent. Every failure mode — config disabled, consent missing, route or ledger denied, permission denied, the host call throwing, usage unreconciled, or the 2-second deadline — records a single skip-… reason and moves on. The hook fires the observation WITHOUT awaiting it: the tool call's latency is unchanged, the observer bounds its own wait at 2s (AbortController), abandoned calls settle their own ledger reservation in the background, and nothing is ever retried or queued.

Shadow never blocks. The only verdict this phase can produce is observe, recorded as a shadow record (point: 'J1', mode: 'shadow', effect: 'none') in the in-memory, bounded decision telemetry collector the plugin never reads back. A high risk score changes the recorded reason and nothing else. The flag verdict is a named constant reserved for a future active phase and is unreachable; there is no deny path, no ask path, and no permission narrowing on this surface.

docs.title: J2 skill-selection scorecard (offline harness)
docs.text:
The skill-selection surface — the P2 local prefilter plus the mode: "skills" preset — is measured by a dated, rerunnable scorecard (bench/results/j2-skill-selection-scorecard-2026-11-03.md), produced by the offline harness tests/pantheon/j2-skill-selection-scorecard.test.ts with its scenario catalog and canned-reply table in tests/pantheon/j2-fixtures.ts. Every scenario runs BOTH paths: the deterministic prefilter (selectPantheonSkills) and the full preset through the real gate chain (config → consent → budget reservation → permission kill-switch → one host call → settlement) on a sandboxed HOME, with globalThis.fetch a throwing spy.

Replies are faked offline. Every Jev answer in the harness comes from a canned, per-scenario table (successes, low confidence, refusals, duplicates, out-of-pool choices, timeouts, malformed payloads) — the harness measures the plumbing (preparation, gating, consumption, telemetry at point J2), not model quality. The states are synthetic by construction and the harness asserts injection prose planted in a state never escapes the state slot into the option pool, the question, the advice, the permission request, or telemetry (leak count 0), and that refusals and timeouts are handled without retrying or throwing into the host.

Activation gate. This phase measures only. The gate is: shadow → 2 consecutive scorecards with the activation criterion met → then, and only then, discuss activation as a separately reviewed change. The criterion is deliberately not defined numerically here, and an offline scorecard proves nothing about the live model — a live, consented, clock-bounded scorecard is a future run.

Question-phrasing finding. One sentence distinguishing required vs preferred attributes measurably doubled answer accuracy in the source measurement (the writing-a-jev-question guide in the awesome-typesafe-jev repository, where the finding originates); apply it when phrasing or revising the mode: "skills" preset instructions.

docs.title: J3 turn-complexity escalation (shadow)
docs.text:
A third, opt-in consumer of the gate chain — and the first Jev uplift surface that computes (but does not apply) a routing decision. When PANTHEON_J3_ESCALATION is set to 1, on, or true (anything else, or unset, leaves it off — off means zero overhead: no sink, no observer, no per-dispatch work), the plugin's execute.before hook fires ONE bounded native Jev decision per delegate dispatch — the native subagent tool assembling the Brief — through the same shared runner (runGatedNativeJevCall): config enabled + egress_consent, budget-ledger admission, the decision.egress permission kill-switch, one host call, settlement.

Classification. The request asks ONE score question — "complexity of this delegation for the current task" — over the full 2..10 level bound (labels trivial … sprawling). The consumer takes the reported score at face value under the tool's own strict validation (name and type must match the prepared question, score non-negative and finite, duplicates refused); anything else is null, never a guess.

Sanitization contract (identical to J1). The request carries NO user content: no Brief text, no task description, no paths. The state text is the exact bounded template over four structural fields — the delegate id (accepted only as a canonical Pantheon agent token; anything else is INPUT_INVALID), the sha256 of the Brief text, its character length, and the local risk-word boolean. The Brief text itself never leaves this machine.

Rails (all local, no Jev call). Three independent local rails force the verdict to the main model regardless of the reported score:

  1. Risk words — the Brief mentioning any of deploy, migrate, drop, delete, prod, production, payment, secret, credential never goes cheap (case-insensitive substring match on purpose: inflections and plurals rail too, and over-matching biases to the safe direction).
  2. User-pinned model — an explicit per-agent override for the delegate in the project model configuration (the same file pantheon_model writes) is never overridden; a configuration that cannot be read counts as pinned.
  3. Context length — a Brief longer than 8,000 chars never downgrades.

Verdict policy. Pure and fail-safe: complexity ≤ 4 (the documented cheap threshold — the lower third of the offered scale, deliberately conservative because a wrong cheap costs task quality while a wrong main only costs tokens) AND no rail tripped → cheap; anything else — including every unsure, malformed, refused or timed-out classification — → main. The main model is never downgraded by uncertainty.

Shadow contract. In this phase the verdict NEVER changes the dispatched model. The record (point: 'J3', mode: 'shadow', effect: 'none', reason tokens like esc-cheap-c2, esc-main-c7, esc-main-c-na, skip-timeout) is the whole effect. The activation mechanism — set the per-agent override for the delegate BEFORE dispatch through the existing model-override mechanism (v2-model-overrides), restore the previous model after — exists in jev-escalation.ts (applyEscalationOverride / clearEscalationOverride) but the shadow observer has no path to it; the plugin wiring carries no reference to it (asserted structurally by the contract test). The mechanism is proved by direct test exercise only: a cheap override resolves to the documented cheap model (opencode/mimo-v2.6-flash, a supported chat model validated by the same capability table the override mechanism uses — decision models are not chat models and are never escalation targets, and the host catalog is never consulted), and clears to the exact previous model. The parent model is never touched by any of this: escalation applies only to delegate dispatches, explicitly.

No delay. Fired without awaiting the hook; self-bounded at 2s (AbortController); on timeout records skip-timeout. In an active phase the same deadline is the dispatch rule: a classification still in flight when the dispatch resolves the model is main — dispatch is never delayed. Exactly one call per dispatch: no retry, no queue.

Activation prerequisites. This phase measures only. Before anything activates: a measured baseline scorecard from replayed synthetic scenarios (the offline harness tests/pantheon/jev-escalation.test.ts proves the plumbing and the rails; it does NOT measure model quality — the request carries structural fields only, so the live classifier's accuracy against real Briefs is unknown until replayed with consented live replies), the shadow-record distribution reviewed, and the activation itself is a separately reviewed change. A quiet log proves nothing — the hermes gate this series adopts.

docs.title: J4 output quality scoring (advisory, on demand)
docs.text:
A fourth consumer of the gate chain — and the first with no flag and no hook: pantheon_jev_decide gains mode: "review", and the review runs ONLY when Zeus explicitly requests it after a delegation completes. That is the reference design's (jev-dsh-decision) on-demand shape: one consented call site (the existing tool, unchanged Zeus-only caller contract and gate chain), one typed round-trip, no automatic observation of delegation traffic.

The review. The request asks TWO questions in the single round-trip: one score — "quality of this delegated result against the criteria", over the full 2..10 rubric bound — and one predicate (noul), "does this result need human review?". The consumer reuses the tool's strict validation (name and type must match the prepared questions, duplicates become errors); anything else is null, never a guess.

Sanitization: criteria in, content never out. The result itself NEVER leaves the machine — the request has no content field at all (structural, not a scrub). The state text is a fixed bounded template over shape metrics only: the delegate id (a canonical Pantheon agent token), the result kind (ok / empty / error), the output character count, the task duration (na when unknown), and the criteria count. The criteria are the ONLY free text admitted, riding the score question's instructions: they are caller-provided instruction strings from the tool schema (never user text), 1–120 chars each. Hostile shapes — paths and path separators, credential assignments and key material (password=…, PEM headers, AWS/SDK/Git token literals, *.key files), control characters, over-length — are rejected CRITERIA_INVALID outright, never sanitized on the way in; any other malformed review input is REVIEW_INPUT_INVALID, refused before any gate work is spent.

DSH hard caps, mirrored. At most 4 criteria per review; bounded instruction strings; exactly ONE call per review (the shared settlement contract: no retry, no queue, fail-closed reservation); redacted errors everywhere — refusals carry reason codes, and a failing host call surfaces the error CLASS only (TypeError, RangeError), never host message text.

Verdict semantics: advisory flag only. The pure verdict (qualityVerdict) is recorded or flag-for-review. An affirmative noul answer is the ONE flagging condition; the flag is advisory telemetry plus a verdict field in the tool output Zeus may weigh — it NEVER blocks, retries, or alters the delegated result. A low quality score with an explicit no-review answer records without flagging: the score is surfaced for Zeus, not enforced. An unsure, malformed, or refused review records na and never flags on a hunch.

Telemetry. One shadow record per review run (point: 'J4', mode: 'shadow', effect: 'none') with a bounded reason token — q-7-review-yes, q-na-review-na, or a skip-… token for every refusal path — into the in-memory, bounded decision telemetry collector the tool path never reads back.

P10 direction. The review's score and flag are the raw material the future P10 counselor-claims layer needs (per-counselor quality claims fed by on-demand reviews). This release wires nothing of the council: no claim is recorded, no counselor reads J4 records, and connecting the two is a separately reviewed change with its own consent surface.

docs.title: Rank and verify (v3.1 primitives)
docs.text: Two further tool modes on pantheon_jev_decide — both built after the review-mode pattern (bounded request built before any gate work, the same shared gate chain, the same refusal contract, the tool's strict answer consumer) and both advisory only: effect stays none, nothing is blocked, dispatched, or altered, and neither mode has a telemetry point (they are tool modes, not shadow gates). Both stay orchestrator-owned: an allowlisted specialist may ask bounded typed questions only.

docs.title: mode: "rank" — pick the best candidate
docs.text:
Input: { schemaVersion: 1, mode: "rank", state, candidates } where state is the usual bounded state text (≤ 12,000 chars, carried verbatim) and candidates is 2–8 records { id, description? } — id a strict bounded token (^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._:-]{0,63}$, unique), description optional bounded prose (≤ 500 chars). The request asks TWO questions in the single round-trip: one choice question (winner) over the candidate ids, and one score question (fit, the 2..10 rubric bound) rating the winner's fit. The tool returns { winner, winnerFit } (each null when the answer is missing, mistyped, duplicated, or an error) plus the usual answers, missing, usage, and frozen fields.

The honest limitation. Rank does NOT return a full ordering, a runner-up, or per-candidate scores. The host Decisions API answers one scalar per question — one score question per candidate would break the 4-question bound above four candidates, and one ambiguous "score each candidate" question has no per-candidate answer structure to pair back. The winner + fit pair is what one typed round-trip can express truthfully; a caller that needs a deeper order uses the explicit-questions mode with its own typed questions.

Sanitization: candidate ids are strict tokens (they become choice values); descriptions are the same sanitization class as J4 criteria — paths, control characters, credential assignments and key material are rejected CANDIDATE_INVALID, never scrubbed; a malformed envelope (unknown keys, missing candidates, count outside 2–8) is RANK_INPUT_INVALID; an invalid state keeps the shared STATE_INVALID token.

docs.title: mode: "verify" — check named claims, fail-closed
docs.text:
Input: { schemaVersion: 1, mode: "verify", claims, state? } where claims is 1–4 named { name, claim } records (token names, bounded claim text). The optional state is caller-supplied EVIDENCE the claims are judged against (bounded, hostility-scanned) — field report beta.13: without it, environment-dependent claims are unanswerable and the honest verdict is UNVERIFIABLE, not FAIL. Verdicts: probability > 0.65 → PASS; 0.35–0.65 → UNVERIFIABLE (the model could not tell — inclusive band, QA beta.20); below → FAIL; and every refusal, timeout, or malformed answer is BLOCK (fail-closed — only PASS counts as passing).

  • probability ≥ 0.5 → PASS;
  • probability < 0.5 → FAIL;
  • a host refusal answer, a timeout (missing answer), a duplicate, or any malformed/out-of-range probability → BLOCK.

BLOCK is the fail-closed direction: an unanswered mandatory claim must never read as verified (or as refuted — an unverifiable claim is unverifiable, not false). The tool itself never acts on a verdict; a caller that REQUIRES a verdict (mandatory verification) treats every gate-chain refusal — which never reaches the consumer — as BLOCK at its own call site. Sanitization is the J4 criteria class: hostile claim shapes (paths, control characters, credential assignments, key material) are rejected CLAIM_INVALID, never scrubbed; a malformed envelope is VERIFY_INPUT_INVALID.

docs.title: Fast decision paths
docs.text:
The decision layers are ordered by cost; use the cheapest one that answers:

Layer Cost Use for Local deterministic selector free, no network per-turn skill/specialist prefilter, marker, skill-array narrowing Jev preset (mode: "skills" / "delegation") one typed call (~150 ms class) stacking skills for a task, picking a specialist with probabilities and confidence, on demand Explicit typed questions one typed call any bounded choice/score/yes-no the orchestrator wants judged Main chat model full model call open-ended reasoning — never replaced by the layers above

docs.title: Candidate expansions (mapped, deliberately unwired)
docs.text:
Each row names the decision, the Jev question, and what must be proven before wiring. None is authorized by this release; every one needs its own carrier measurement, consent/payload policy, and review — the same bar the tool itself went through.

Candidate Jev question Why it could help Must be proven first Memory persistence advisory predicate: "is this state worth a durable entry?" fewer missed saves and less noise the measured save-moment carrier; the advisory must never relax the explicit request/authorization rule Council pre-ranking choice over counselors cheaper assembly for genuinely multi-perspective work a real council carrier (the council point is still unwired) Vision-call gating predicate before vision_describe probably none — vision already fires only for image jobs; an extra decision adds latency a measured case of vision invoked without an image driver Per-agent affordances specialists' own typed questions parallel small decisions off the main model caller-matrix policy, per-agent consent, review Skill discovery tool search the ecosystem from the session removes the manual npx skills find step its own networked-egress consent surface and a registry trust policy

Until one of these is wired, the flow stays: local prefilter → Jev preset (consented) → main model, with MCP calls governed by their own documented policies (memory: explicit request/authorization; vision: image-driven; persistence: explicit checkpoints).

docs.title: Provider matrix (measured on the 2.2.5 host binary)
docs.text: The host embeds decision modules for exactly 8 providerIDs: opencode, typesafe-ai, openrouter, vercel-ai-gateway, cloudflare-workers-ai, cloudflare-ai-gateway, baseten, digitalocean. There is no openai, zen, microsoft or laya module — those backends are only reachable via a plugin's own transport (the OpenAI Decisions protocol is a different one; the host does not speak it). Decision models are not chat models: none of the jev models appear in opencode models regardless of provider. Expansion is table-only on Pantheon's side — the host normalizes every embedded provider behind the same decisions call.

docs.title: Candidate expansions (2026-11-04, mapped, deliberately unwired)
docs.text:
• OpenAI Decisions protocol — the host 2.2.5 has no openai decisions module; OpenAI speaks a different protocol (POST api.openai.com/v1/decisions, model gpt-6-luna, up to 400 questions, refusal as an answer type). Wiring it means Pantheon running its own transport for the first time — breaks the "egress only via the host native route" principle. Deliberately unwired.
  • What's-new window — a one-time TUI notice on version change surfacing the changelog highlights (the extractor exists: scripts/changelog-extract.mjs). Planned.

docs.title: Specialist callers (shipped)
docs.text: PANTHEON_JEV_SPECIALIST_CALLERS (CSV, default empty = Zeus only) allowlists agents to call pantheon_jev_decide with explicit typed questions; preset modes (skills/delegation/review/rank/verify) stay orchestrator-owned. The permission assertion and the success output carry the real caller; caps and the decision.egress kill-switch are enforced per call regardless of caller.

docs.title: Skill ecosystem (hybrid, on-demand)
docs.text:
The stacking preset is open: its pool is the Pantheon catalog plus every skill the host has installed (ctx.skill.list()). Anything following the open Agent Skills format (SKILL.md) — Pantheon's own or third-party — becomes decidable the moment it is installed, with no Pantheon change.

Division of labor; trusting an install is never the model's job:

  • Install — reviewed and project-isolated. npx skills add <repo> -a opencode -y (the open skills ecosystem CLI) places the skill strictly in the project's skill directory (<project>/.agents/skills/). Global installation is disallowed for project capabilities to avoid environment contamination. Third-party skills are untrusted instructions: review the SKILL.md and any scripts before installing, prefer pinned versions, and keep production servers off ad-hoc installs.
  • Decide — with the pool installed, mode: "skills" pre-filters local candidates (or offers the whole pool) and Jev picks what to stack for the current task in one typed call; the answer is advisory and loads nothing.
  • Share — a private skills repository (for example ils15/pantheon-skills) becomes the approved, versioned library other projects pull from; the skills CLI resolves private repositories with existing git credentials.

The discovery pipeline binds these steps into one measured ladder (zeus.md carries the same rules):

  1. mode: "skills" answers over the installed pool — the Jev call that decides within existing skills.
  2. Only on a gap: one read-only search across the trust cascade — node scripts/skill-search.mjs "<query>" --limit 5 queries, in order: the canonical Anthropic catalog (anthropics/skills — curated upstream; checked first so the canonical pdf/docx/mcp-builder skills outrank the third-party clones that popularity ranking surfaces), the skills.sh index (breadth with install-count signal, unreviewed; known-good community repos to try by name in the GitHub tier: mattpocock/skills — engineering craft, still untrusted until reviewed), and raw GitHub filename:SKILL.md code search (orders of magnitude wider — 8,480 hits for "satellite" where the skills.sh index offered three — and the weakest trust). Output is the merged parseable contract ({skill, installs, url, source} JSON; pinned by tests/skill-search.test.mjs), tier-ordered. The search is networked egress by the agent, priced by attention — never a Jev question by itself, and at most one per need.
  3. One typed Jev choice question ranks the returned candidates (descriptions + install counts as choice text; "none of these fit" is a valid answer). Only names, counts and short descriptions cross the boundary — skill contents are untrusted and never enter a Jev call.
  4. The winning candidate(s) are PROACTIVELY presented to the user via the native question tool with 1-click execution options. Zeus never instructs the user to run terminal commands; upon the user's approval in the interactive gate, Zeus dispatches an execution specialist with bash permissions (@hermes or @talos) to execute npx skills add <owner/repo@skill> -a opencode -y strictly in the project root (.agents/skills/). The installed skill joins the local pool that step 1 answers over.

docs.title: Verification boundary
docs.text: The focused tests (tests/pantheon/jev-decisions.test.ts, tests/pantheon/v2-native-decisions.test.ts, tests/pantheon/jev-rank-verify.test.ts) are offline: the native API is a typed stub, the budget ledger runs on a temp database, and the success path runs with globalThis.fetch replaced by a throwing spy to prove the native route never touches a transport. A real-host canary asserts the tool's registration. No live provider request, canary, or credential check has been performed. The manual pantheon_local_decision advisory tool remains local-only and separate. Field validation evidence lives in dated records under bench/results/ (see jev-field-validation-2026-11-05.md for the sandbox install, the live scorecard, the N4 re-test, and the verify field run).

docs.title: Expansion verdicts (measured, 2026-11-05)
docs.text:
Each expansion direction was weighed against the measured gate chain and the field validation; the verdicts below are the current standing answer, not a ban — new field evidence reopens them.

  • Jev as the arbiter of native-MCP calls (memory recall/store, checkpoints, code-mode reads): no. The economics are negative — a decide call reserves budget and spends a live route round-trip to gate a free, local, instant call. Where the answer is a rule, the rule wins: usage policy lives in the agent instructions (zeus first, then the roster reform), measured by the MCP usage audit, not by paid arbitration.
  • Jev as the spend gate for pantheon-vision: defer. Vision is the only gateway-costed native MCP, but volume is small (84 execute blocks, 54 calls over the whole field history) and the V1 permission tier (ask) plus the one-pass-per-image usage policy already bound it. Revisit only if the audit shows repeated abuse that rules cannot hold.
  • Rank cap 8→20 (P4/P11 need 20+ candidates): blocked on a design change, not a constant. The host answers one scalar per question, so winner-with-fit-score does not scale past roughly 10 candidates — at 20+ the single question cannot discriminate. Expansion implies a tiered or tournament shape (two rounds of 8, or a shortlist round followed by a winner round), each round its own reserved call; that doubles latency and cost per decision, so it must be its own measured change, not a cap bump.
  • Callers and routes: sufficient. PANTHEON_JEV_SPECIALIST_CALLERS (typed questions for allowlisted specialists), Zeus-only presets, and the five supported routes cover the current usage; no evidence of demand for more.
  • Dead-route holds: releasable, narrowly. decision-router holds release --provider <p> --reason archives and releases unresolved holds of providers that no longer exist (they can never reconcile and would freeze budget forever). Live providers are refused; their holds settle by reconciliation or roll off with the period.

docs.title: Offline evaluation protocol: routing and complexity
docs.text: Status (2026-10-29): protocol only. This document specifies a future offline evaluation; it reports no benchmark results. No local dataset or benchmark has been established, no model calls were made, no provider was selected, and no transfer of data to a provider was authorized. “Offline” means scoring a frozen set of task cases separately from live routing; it does not make a remote model request local or private.

docs.title: Questions and candidates
docs.text:
Compare four candidates on the same held-out cases, but treat these as two independent tasks:

  1. Agent selection/routing: identify the appropriate action (inline, agent, or coordinated actions), or abstain.
  2. Complexity classification: label the task low, medium, or high, or abstain. Do not use a routing decision as the complexity label.
Candidate Evaluation role Primary reference Current dispatcher / baseline track Incumbent dispatch is qualitative. A deterministic rule baseline is not yet defined or approved, so this track has no scoreable baseline output. src/agents/zeus.md; Architecture TypeSafe Jev 1.14 Candidate model TypeSafe models OpenAI Decisions / GPT-6 Luna Candidate model OpenAI Decisions Cloudflare Clef-Flash Candidate model Cloudflare Clef-Flash

The three model entries are candidates, not endorsements, compatibility claims, or a provider choice. Vendor specifications, pricing, and latency are vendor claims, not independent evidence; evaluate quality and measure latency/cost on the same authorized run rather than using catalog claims as results.

docs.title: Incumbent dispatcher and rule-baseline prerequisite
docs.text:
Pantheon's documented dispatcher is qualitative: self-contained work may stay inline; expertise, uncertainty, dependencies, risk, and verifiability inform specialist selection; independent fronts may be dispatched separately; and planning, discovery, or review is added when scope and risk call for it. It does not specify a complete role-to-task mapping, thresholds for ambiguity, or a tie-break rule. It is an incumbent policy reference, not a deterministic baseline, and no performance for it has been measured.

A separate deterministic rule baseline can be scored only after its role map, route/action rules, ambiguity/abstention rule, and treatment of optional review or supporting dispatches are explicitly written and approved as product policy. The current docs do not supply these decisions. This protocol does not invent them: until approval, a deterministic baseline and the empirical candidate comparison must wait. Do not report a qualitative dispatcher judgment as a deterministic baseline result.

docs.title: Reproducible evaluation protocol (prerequisites; not yet run)
docs.text:
Before annotation or scoring, freeze the relevant agent-role descriptions, routing instructions, and approved evaluation rubric. Record the source commit SHA, freeze date, and hashes of the frozen files in the evaluation record; any change requires a new versioned evaluation. No evaluation snapshot is frozen by this document.

For each case, two independently assigned raters annotate the gold route and complexity while blinded to model and baseline outputs. Resolve disagreements with a third, pre-named routing-policy adjudicator who records the rationale and final decision. The raters and adjudicator have not been assigned. If no adjudicator or approved role map is available, do not score that case or claim a benchmark.

Represent the route as required action slots, not one forced winner. Each slot contains the adjudicated set of acceptable role/action alternatives; a multi-front task may have multiple required slots. A prediction satisfies a slot if it selects one member of that slot's accepted set, with each predicted action matched at most once. Unfilled slots are misses; unsupported extra dispatches are false positives. Report slot-level precision/recall/F1 and exact route-set accuracy. Keep optional supporting actions in separate adjudicated slots; do not add alternatives or resolve ties after seeing model outputs. If raters cannot agree on acceptable alternatives after adjudication, mark the case unresolved, exclude it from the primary score, and report it separately.

The following is a proposed evaluation rubric, not existing Pantheon policy; its approval is a prerequisite to any empirical run. Independently score each dimension as 0, 1, or 2 using the frozen task context:

Dimension 0 1 2 Boundedness Localized, explicit scope Bounded but spans components Broad, unclear, or unbounded scope Reversibility Straightforward rollback Reversible with planned migration/coordination Hard to reverse or materially irreversible Dependencies None or direct Known local sequencing Cross-front, sequential, or unknown dependencies Uncertainty Requirements and context clear Limited, bounded unknowns Material unresolved requirements/context Verification Direct focused check Several component-level checks Broad integration or extensive independent verification Sensitive-gate status No security/auth/data-integrity gate identified Required review gate Explicit human authorization required or gate status unresolved

Assign low only when all dimensions are 0; medium when no dimension is 2 and at least one is 1; high when any dimension is 2. If required context is missing, retain the uncertainty score and mark the case for adjudication rather than guessing. Record sensitive-gate status separately alongside the complexity label. These labels never remove or relax a gate, authorize work, grant shell, or change approval requirements; security and authorization remain orthogonal controls for every label.

There is no local annotated dataset, approved task-to-role routing map, assigned rater/adjudicator, or approved rubric at present. These are open prerequisites, not completed work.

docs.title: Dataset and run protocol
docs.text:
1. Curate only after authorization. No local dataset currently exists. Prefer synthetic or explicitly approved, non-sensitive task summaries. Do not include source code, secrets, personal data, private repository details, or full conversation history unless separately reviewed and authorized.
  2. Create labels before model evaluation. Follow the blinded two-rater and named-adjudicator procedure above. Record evidence for each label, acceptable route sets, gate status, and reviewer agreement. Keep any approved rule baseline output separate from gold labels.
  3. Hold out by group, not by random prompt. Keep related issues, tasks from the same project/family, and near-duplicates in one split. Use a development set for prompt/schema iteration and confidence thresholds; seal a final holdout by project/family or time. Do not tune against holdout results. Report actual counts and class balance; if there are too few independent groups or examples, report the evaluation as exploratory, not conclusive.
  4. Freeze the interface. Give every candidate the same minimal task text, relevant documented agent-role descriptions, rubric, and output schema. Freeze prompts/adapters before holdout evaluation. Require structured output with route/label, concise evidence, and abstention reason; reject invalid output and send it to human review rather than repairing it silently. Use a deterministic fallback only if a rule baseline has been separately approved.
  5. Keep tracks separate. Score routing against adjudicated route slots and score complexity against its independent labels. Only after the rule baseline is approved, run it and each model on identical cases; randomize case order and avoid carrying conversation state between cases.
  6. Log one reproducible record per case: anonymized case ID and split, prompt/schema hash, model/provider identifier and immutable version or snapshot (where offered), API version, SDK/runtime version, date/region, generation settings, response validity, abstention/fallback, measured latency, and measured token/cost fields when available. Mark unavailable fields; do not infer them from marketing material.

For provider-hosted candidates, an evaluation run still sends request data to that provider. It requires a separate explicit decision on data scope, provider, region, retention, credentials, and call budget before any calls. Use no credentials or network calls as part of this protocol-only change.

docs.title: Metrics and decision rules
docs.text:
Report per candidate and per track, with raw counts and confusion matrices; include uncertainty intervals grouped by project/task family where sample size permits. Do not combine routing and complexity into one score.

Track Primary measures Error/coverage measures Routing Required-slot precision/recall/F1; exact route-set accuracy Per-agent confusion; unnecessary/missed supporting dispatches; abstention and invalid-output rates; selective error among non-abstained cases Complexity Macro-F1 and balanced accuracy Ordinal weighted agreement and mean absolute ordinal error; over/under-classification; abstention and invalid-output rates

Report task-level latency (median and p95), measured token usage and cost per case, failure/retry rates, and quality-versus-cost trade-offs alongside quality; do not substitute embedding similarity for either routing correctness or complexity. Treat self-reported confidence as uncalibrated. If a candidate returns a probability/confidence score, assess calibration (for example Brier score or expected calibration error) on development data and report its limitations; otherwise do not use self-reported confidence to set a threshold. Set any abstention thresholds on development data only, report coverage against error, and route low-confidence, malformed, or out-of-distribution cases to human review or the approved deterministic rule baseline, if one exists. Do not silently convert abstentions into confident labels.

Pre-register acceptance criteria before unsealing the holdout. A candidate is not suitable merely because its aggregate score is higher: examine per-class errors and high-impact cases, and require no model output to bypass human approval or existing gates. Publish sample counts and limitations; if the holdout is underpowered or results are inconclusive, report no winner. If no approved deterministic baseline exists, do not run or publish the empirical candidate comparison.

docs.title: Safety and current non-authorization
docs.text:
• JEV remains disabled by default and opt-in only. This protocol does not enable it, change runtime behavior, or authorize its use. The sanctioned activation path is the explicit pantheon_jev_decide tool behind its own consent, budget, and permission chain — see V2 Native Decisions.
  • Bifrost is research-only here, not an evaluation or production runtime.
  • Model output may be an advisory label only. It cannot change grants, invoke shell, approve work, alter permissions/policy, or dispatch automatically.
  • No provider has been selected. Any future live evaluation, credentials, dataset transfer, or rollout needs its own authorization and appropriate privacy/security review.

docs.title: Primary references
docs.text:
Official vendor documentation supplied for this protocol; checked as references on 2026-10-29. Vendor documentation is not independent benchmark evidence:

  • TypeSafe models
  • OpenAI Decisions
  • Cloudflare Workers AI: Clef-Flash

docs.title: Update — 2.0 cycle (2026-11)
docs.text: The structural track is now REAL: golden positive/negative evals over the actual generators run in the regular node tier (tests/eval/instruction-golden.test.mjs — managed-region carve, zero-overlap of shared instructions, agent-scoped routing, deterministic line budget). The model-in-the-loop track (routing slots, complexity rubric, hold-out metrics) remains gated by this protocol: it needs the curated dataset, ratified raters/adjudicator and an authorized provider before any run. The completion stub used by the host harness is now a shared fixture (dev/tests/shared/fake-completion-server.mjs); a nightly host-backed run stays behind workflow_dispatch with the SKIP-labeled convention (a skip is never a PASS).

docs.title: Performance and tuning
docs.text: Measured costs of the orchestration layer and the knobs that change them. Nothing here changes security semantics; every gate keeps its default.

docs.title: Where the time goes
docs.text: Cost Status Notes Secret scan per tool call in-process since beta.8 Was one bash spawn per tool call (scan-secrets.sh); now pattern matching inside the plugin (v2-hook-engine.ts), same exit-code contract and fail-closed classifier. Delegation audit per dispatch in-process since beta.8 The start/stop bash scripts (which also spawned python3 each) now write the same delegations.log JSON lines directly. Post-write formatting spawns only when applicable format-multi-language.sh runs only for edit/write/hashline_edit on formattable extensions (and bash); every other tool call skips it. Todo-enforcer idle check idle-time only Queries session.children() on idle events with a 30 s post-user-message quiet window. Kill-switch: PANTHEON_TODO_ENFORCER=off. Prompt admission hook cheap Local deterministic selection (routing.yml parsed once per process), P1/P2 shadow records in memory. Compaction hook shadow Observes the carrier; injects nothing.

docs.title: Prompt budget (per turn / per dispatch)
docs.text:
Payload Size Knob Zeus system prompt ~17 KB Kept lean by pruning release history; behavior detail lives in skills loaded on demand. Specialist system prompts 3–12 KB Two-tier verification (src/agents/*.md): small bounded fix → one targeted proof; material change → full test discipline. AGENTS.md injection ~1.8 KB Project-owned; regenerated region is install metadata.

Skill stacking is the intended lever: pantheon_jev_decide mode: "skills" picks what to load per task instead of carrying everything always.

docs.title: Decision latency
docs.text:
• Obvious route → dispatch directly (no decision call).
  • Ambiguous route/skill stack → one typed pantheon_jev_decide call (consent- and budget-gated) instead of open-ended orchestrator reasoning.
  • Model tiers: phase reviews on the flash tier; the pro tier reserved for the final gate (routing.yml / set-tier).

docs.title: MCP servers (measured)
docs.text:
Cost Number Note fastmcp import per server 0.5–0.8 s Paid once per host session at server spawn (5 servers ⇒ ~2.5–4 s of Python imports at startup); per-CALL costs are sqlite-local and fast. Startup parallelization is host-side. Memory search FTS5 (BM25) SQLite-side keyword search with freshness decay; the vector pipeline (sqlite-vec + fastembed) is documented as not active — no embedding fallback exists, so storage shape matters (see MEMORY.md). Vision deps heavy (separate venv) Installed only with the runtime component; the vision server is the reason --no-mcp exists.

Improvement queue (deliberately not done): an embeddings pipeline for memory (needs model + storage decisions), and host-side server warm-start. Neither is a per-call latency problem today.

docs.title: Skill discovery (designed, unwired)
docs.text: The three-tier skill provenance search — installed / registry / ecosystem, with Jev ranking annotated candidates and trust staying outside the model — is specified in Skill search design. Tier 1 (local only) could ship without any new consent surface; tiers 2–3 need the egress class described there.

docs.title: Context growth (long sessions)
docs.text: The deterministic context pruner exists but is off by default (per-request pruning invalidates the provider prompt cache; enabling it trades cache hits for smaller payloads). Enable explicitly when sessions routinely outgrow the window; compaction remains the host's own mechanism.

docs.title: Skill provenance search with Jev — investigation
docs.text: Status: design only. Deliberately unwired. This document specifies what a skill-discovery layer would be, what Jev's role in it is (and is not), and the consent surface it requires. Nothing here is implemented; wiring it needs its own review, exactly like the native Decisions tool did.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: An agent that needs a capability has three disjoint sources today: the Pantheon catalog (fixed), the skills installed in the host (visible via ctx.skill.list()), and the open ecosystem (skills.sh and arbitrary repos), which is reachable only by a human running npx skills find. Nothing tells the agent what exists, where a candidate came from, or whether it was reviewed.

docs.title: Design shape
docs.text:
A pantheon_skill_search advisory tool (Zeus-first, same caller-matrix rule as pantheon_jev_decide) over THREE tiers, each answer carrying PROVENANCE:

Tier Source Provenance fields Network 1. Installed ctx.skill.list() skill id, install path, host none 2. Registry a Pantheon-approved registry (e.g. ils15/pantheon-skills) repo@commit, reviewed-by, date git fetch, opt-in flag 3. Ecosystem skills.sh / npx skills find output repo, stars/metadata, UNREVIEWED flag networked, separate explicit consent

Jev's role is deliberately narrow: given the task state and a bounded candidate list WITH provenance attached, a typed choice question picks which candidate merits loading — the same stack-the-skills decision the preset makes today, extended with the provenance tier as a visible field. Jev NEVER fetches, evaluates code, or vouches for trust; a rank from tier 3 is always labeled UNREVIEWED in the answer.

docs.title: Why Jev and not a bigger model
docs.text: Ranking a short annotated candidate list is exactly the System One shape: one typed call, ~150 ms class, no open-ended generation. The expensive part — reading a SKILL.md and judging quality — stays a human/dispatched-agent task.

docs.title: Consent surface (the reason this is unwired)
docs.text: Tier 2/3 create a NEW egress class: networked queries with attacker-influenced content (registry metadata, ecosystem listings). Wiring requires: an explicit skill.search.egress permission action (same kill-switch pattern as decision.egress), a per-tier consent flag in the decision-router config, a payload policy (query text only — no task content, no code), a result-size bound, and the Themis review the native tool went through. Tier 1 alone needs none of that and could ship as a pure local ranking — the recommended first step if this is built.

docs.title: Provenance schema (proposal)
docs.text:
{
  "id": "docker-build-strategies",
  "tier": "ecosystem",
  "origin": { "repo": "docker/skills", "commit": "abc1234", "path": "..." },
  "reviewed": { "by": "human|agent", "date": "2026-11-02", "verdict": "approved|quarantine" },
  "installedAt": "2026-11-02T09:00:00Z"
}

The registry repo is where review verdicts live; installs copy the verdict forward. An UNREVIEWED ecosystem skill is decidable but labeled — the user decides whether to install, which is the trust boundary that stays outside the model.

docs.title: The What's-new TUI window
docs.text: When the Pantheon version changes since the last TUI start, the OpenCode V2 TUI shows a one-time, dismissable "O que há de novo — Pantheon <version>" dialog listing the highlights for that version, taken from the CHANGELOG.md section of the running version (H3 subsection headings plus their bullets, at most 12 bullets, reduced to plain text). Dismiss it with esc or q; the version is then recorded and the window never appears again until the next version — including downgrades, which also count as a change.

docs.title: Where the seen-version lives
docs.text:
<configDir>/.pantheon/whats-new.json, next to the other OpenCode-level Pantheon state (install-state.json, the active-preset file). <configDir> resolves like the rest of the installer: $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/opencode, then the legacy ~/.opencode when that is what exists. The file is one small JSON document written atomically (unique temp file + rename):

{ "seenVersion": "1.6.3-beta.4", "updatedAt": "2026-11-04T12:00:00.000Z" }

docs.title: Re-showing a window
docs.text:
The window is keyed by version, not by a flag, so there is nothing to toggle in the configuration:

  • Re-show the current version's window: delete the state file (or remove the seenVersion field) and restart OpenCode:
rm ~/.config/opencode/.pantheon/whats-new.json
  • Never show it again for this version: dismiss it once (esc/q), or pre-seed seenVersion with the running version.

docs.title: Failure behavior
docs.text: The window is a nicety and fails open everywhere: a missing or corrupt state file reads as "never seen" (the window may show), a failed write is silent, and a missing or unreadable CHANGELOG.md, an unknown version, or a section with no bullets all mean the window simply does not show. Nothing here can block or break TUI startup. The window exists in the V2 generation (dist/tui-v2.js); the legacy V1 generation does not show it. CHANGELOG.md ships at the plugin copy root (<configDir>/plugins/pantheon-tui/CHANGELOG.md) so the window can read the release notes offline.

docs.title: Pantheon 1.6.0
docs.text: Release notes for the 1.6.0 candidate. This page is the short version; the changelog is the complete record.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• OpenCode 2 works, and auto picks the plugin generation from the host.
  • V2 tools now run instead of only announcing success.
  • Three permission gaps are closed.
  • Cost reporting answers money questions by model and by session.
  • The installer is reviewable and reversible.

docs.title: Upgrade actions
docs.text:
• Update: npm install -g pantheon-opencode@beta && pantheon-opencode update.
  • Refresh config: pantheon-opencode init --yes --headless.
  • Verify: pantheon-opencode doctor.
  • Pin a generation: npx pantheon-opencode init --opencode-version v2.

docs.title: What's new by capability
docs.text:
• V2 support: auto prefers explicit input, then the environment, then a host probe; an unreadable host warns once.
  • Permissions: agent MCP allowlists become native rules that deny by default.
  • Permissions: read-only agents cannot reach mutating tools on either generation.
  • Cost: reports add USD, per-model and per-session views.
  • Cost: session scopes a report to a root session and its descendants.
  • Memory: entries are capped at 64 KiB and can expire; search failures return a typed error.
  • Installer: apply previews each file, detects drift, and keeps an exact backup.
  • Installer: restore, reconcile and uninstall cover recovery and removal.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text:
• V2 tools no longer report success without executing.
  • Empty child dispatch results surface as errors.
  • Offline cost mode refuses an explicit price refresh.

docs.title: V2 compatibility
docs.text: OpenCode 1.19.x (V1) and OpenCode 2.x (V2) are supported; 2.0.22 is known broken. See Compatibility for the policy and verified-version evidence.

docs.title: Deprecated & removed
docs.text:
• V1 goal tools are soft-deprecated and no longer auto-continue a session.
  • The legacy vector memory path and V2 goal tools are gone.
  • Persistence no longer exposes twelve KV/context-management tools.

See UPGRADING.md for the exact steps.

docs.title: Known issues
docs.text:
• ask is not expressible for MCP on OpenCode 2.x; the installer warns and emits no rule.
  • hashline_edit and vision_describe have no host permission gate.

Full changelog: CHANGELOG.md — v1.6.0
